Two callers that both read CAPTURED_HOLD before either writes REFUND_PENDING both reach stripe.refunds.create with the full amount and both pass the maxRefundable check (both saw refunded_amount = 0).
Partial mitigation the claim did not credit: if the loser's transitionPaymentStatus read lands AFTER the winner's write, canTransition(REFUND_PENDING, REFUND_PENDING) is false (paymentStateMachine.js:84-87) and it throws, refundForBooking catches and logs (schedulingPaymentsService.js:137-140). Reachability confirmed: POST /api/public/booking/:token/cancel is unauthenticated (backend/routes/schedulingPublic.js:459-469, manage-token only), guarded by bookingWriteLimiter = 20 writes / 10 min (backend/middleware/rateLimiter.js:272-280), and both requests return 200 with status 'cancelled'.

evidence:
Traced end to end in the working tree (the claim's line numbers are stale; the handler is now at backend/routes/schedulingPublic.js:472-481).

It calls loadByManageToken (353-365), which resolves a BookingToken by sha256 hash and kind='manage' and returns the booking; the only property proven is 'the caller holds a manage token for this booking row'. It then does `hashEmail(ctx.booking.invitee_email)` (475) and inserts into EmailSuppression (478). The invitee_email on that row came straight from the unauthenticated create-booking body: createSchema only validates syntax (`email: Joi.string().email().max(320).required()`, 195) and POST /book/:slug/:eventTypeSlug never verifies control of the address — it only *attributes* the booking to req.user when the signed-in email matches (305-306), which an anonymous caller simply skips. The manage token is handed back in the 201 body (`manageToken: result.manageToken`, 336; same at 287 for the one-off route), so one unauthenticated POST yields a manage token bound to an arbitrary victim address.
The suppression is global, not scoped: EmailSuppression has exactly (id, email_hash, reason, created_at) with no booking/page/owner column (backend/database/migrations/161_calendarly_packages_automations.sql:94-100) and a UNIQUE index on email_hash alone (161:212). isEmailSuppressed(email) (backend/services/scheduling/schedulingShared.js:114-120) filters on email_hash only and is consulted for every non-user invitee reminder (backend/services/scheduling/bookingNotifyService.js:310-311, `if (await isEmailSuppressed(booking.invitee_email)) return;`).
No undo path: `grep -rn EmailSuppression backend/` returns only schedulingPublic.js:476/478 and schedulingShared.js:117 — one select, one insert, one check. There is no delete, no resubscribe route, no admin path.
Full attack: POST /api/public/book/<live-slug>/<free-event-type> {name:'x', email:'victim@example.com', start_at:<free slot>} -> 201 with manageToken; POST /api/public/booking/<manageToken>/unsubscribe -> 200 {ok:true}; POST .../cancel to release the slot. sha256('victim@example.com') is now permanently in EmailSuppression and every future reminder for that address as a non-signed-in invitee, on any host's page, is dropped. Rate limit is 20 writes/10 min per IP (backend/middleware/rateLimiter.js:272-280), i.e. ~6 victims per window per IP at 3 requests each.
One scope correction to the claim: suppression only affects REMINDER email (bookingNotifyService.js:311); lifecycle mail (confirmation/cancel/reschedule) at 220-241 is not gated by it. Impact is permanent loss of appointment reminders for the victim, not total mail loss.

(1) Add `owner_type`/`owner_id` (or `booking_id`) to EmailSuppression, drop the email_hash-only UNIQUE for a UNIQUE(email_hash, owner_type, owner_id), insert with that scope in schedulingPublic.js:478, and give isEmailSuppressed(email, ownerType, ownerId) the matching filter at schedulingShared.js:114-120 with bookingNotifyService.js:311 passing the booking's owner. (2) Stop returning manageToken in the create-booking 201 for callers whose email is unverified (schedulingPublic.js:336 and 287) — deliver the manage link only in the confirmation email, which bookingNotifyService.js:122 already builds. (3) Add a resubscribe/delete endpoint so a suppression is reversible.

evidence:
backend/services/scheduling/packageService.js:81-87 restoreForBooking reads `remaining` at 83 and writes `remaining: credit.remaining + 1` at 85 with only `.eq('id', credit.id)` — no CAS, in direct contrast to its sibling redeemForBooking which does guard with `.eq('remaining', credit.remaining)` at 68. One PackageCredit row is a pack of N sessions shared by many bookings (packageService.js:25/50 insert total = pkg.sessions_count, remaining = same), so two bookings legitimately point at the same credit row and concurrent restores are ordinary, not exotic. Callers are bookingService.js:364 (declineBooking) and :387 (cancelBooking), both reachable concurrently — cancelBooking from the unauthenticated token route (backend/routes/schedulingPublic.js:459) and from the owner route, with no serialization anywhere (see the cancel-toctou finding: the booking UPDATE itself has no status guard, so both cancels run their side effects).
Concrete loss: pack of 5, 3 booked (remaining = 2). Two of those bookings are cancelled concurrently; both restore calls read remaining = 2 and both write 3. The buyer ends with 3 usable credits instead of 4, unrecoverable without manual DB repair.
fix: Use the same optimistic CAS as redeemForBooking: `.update({ remaining: credit.remaining + 1 }).eq('id', credit.id).eq('remaining', credit.remaining).select('id')` and retry (bounded) when zero rows come back. Cleaner: a single-statement RPC `UPDATE "PackageCredit" SET remaining = remaining + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND remaining < total`.

evidence:
Both emitters compute SEQUENCE as a boolean: backend/services/scheduling/bookingNotifyService.js:99 `sequence: booking.previous_start_at ? 1 : 0` and backend/routes/schedulingPublic.js:436 (same expression, in the /booking/:token/ics download). backend/services/scheduling/bookingService.js:457 sets `previous_start_at: booking.start_at` on EVERY reschedule and there is no counter column — `grep -n ics_sequence` across backend/database/migrations/*.sql and backend/services returns nothing; the only revision-ish column is previous_start_at (160_calendarly_bookings.sql:66). buildIcs faithfully emits what it is handed with a stable UID: `UID:${uid}@pantopus.com` (icsService.js:88) and `SEQUENCE:${sequence}` (icsService.js:89). So the 2nd, 3rd, Nth reschedule all ship SEQUENCE:1 under the same UID, and RFC 5546 requires an iTIP REQUEST that is not strictly newer than the stored SEQUENCE to be treated as out of date. The CANCEL case is worse: a never-rescheduled booking's METHOD:CANCEL carries SEQUENCE:0, identical to its original REQUEST.
Failure path is exactly as described: Tue->Wed reschedule mails SEQUENCE:1 (accepted); Wed->Thu mails SEQUENCE:1 again (dropped by Outlook/Apple Calendar/ical4j). The guest's calendar keeps Wed while the app shows Thu.
fix: Persist a monotonic revision on Booking (`ALTER TABLE "Booking" ADD COLUMN ics_sequence integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`), increment it in the same UPDATE as every mutating transition (rescheduleBooking bookingService.js:452-463, cancelBooking 388-393, declineBooking 365-370, approveBooking 349-353), and pass `booking.ics_sequence` as `sequence` from bookingNotifyService.js:99 and schedulingPublic.js:436.

evidence:
Every link in the chain checks out.
(1) Priced bookings are inserted 'pending': backend/services/scheduling/bookingService.js:191-193 `const priced = payments.isPriced(eventType); const status = priced || eventType.requires_approval ? 'pending' : 'confirmed';`. The row commits at 220 BEFORE the PaymentIntent is created at 256-271, and the rollback there only covers a failed intent creation — an intent that is created and then abandoned by the user leaves the row.
(2) A pending row occupies the slot: the Booking_no_overlap GiST exclusion predicate is `status IN ('pending','confirmed') AND enforce_exclusive` (backend/database/migrations/160_calendarly_bookings.sql:255-266) and the availability engine filters the same set (availabilityService busy query, see 160:222 index), so the slot vanishes from the public grid and blocks every other booker.
(3) Nothing ever expires it. `grep -rn booking_payment backend/ --include=*.js` outside tests returns only schedulingPaymentsService.js:4 (comment) and :61 (the tag write) — no job, webhook or route reads it. The only auth sweeper is backend/jobs/expireUncapturedAuthorizations.js, which is strictly gig-shaped: for every AUTHORIZED payment it does `.from('Gig').select(...).eq('id', payment.gig_id).single()` (54-58, and again 187-191) and hits `if (!gig) { logger.warn('gig not found'); continue; }` (60-63) — booking payments are created with `gigId: null` (schedulingPaymentsService.js:46), so they always take that branch. `grep -rln "from('Booking')" backend/jobs/` returns only bookingReminders.js, which just sends mail for confirmed bookings (backend/jobs/bookingReminders.js:38-43).
Result: an invitee who receives the clientSecret and closes the tab leaves a permanent pending row that blocks the slot for everyone, that the host cannot approve (capture fails — capturePayment requires payment_status AUTHORIZED, stripeService.js:1084-1086), and that no job cleans up.
fix: Add a booking-payment sweeper (new job, or a Part 3 in expireUncapturedAuthorizations): select Payments with `payment_type = 'booking_payment'` and payment_status in (AUTHORIZE_PENDING, AUTHORIZED) whose Booking is still 'pending' past a short TTL (~30 min for never-confirmed intents, authorization_expires_at for authorized ones), call stripeService.cancelAuthorization, and transition the Booking to 'cancelled' so the exclusion range is released. Also guard the existing job with `if (!payment.gig_id) continue;` before the Gig lookups at expireUncapturedAuthorizations.js:54 and :187 so booking payments are routed explicitly rather than warn-and-skipped.

evidence:
backend/routes/schedulingPublic.js:552 (claim said 531): `const voterKey = (req.user && req.user.id) || (req.body.email ? normalizeEmail(req.body.email) : null);` — a bare, unverified, caller-supplied email is accepted as a write identity. pollVoteSchema (543-547) validates only `Joi.string().email()`. The upsert matches on (option_id, voter_key) alone (565) and, when a row exists, overwrites BOTH value and voter_name (567). There is no token, no ownership check, and no signed-in requirement; the route is `router.post('/poll/:id/vote', bookingWriteLimiter, optionalAuth, ...)` on the unauthenticated /api/public mount.
The DB agrees with the app rather than protecting it: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX SchedulingPollVote_unique ON SchedulingPollVote (option_id, voter_key)` (backend/database/migrations/165_calendarly_advanced.sql:169) — one row per (option, claimed email), so the attacker's write lands exactly on the victim's row.
Reconnaissance is free: GET /poll/:id (533-541) is unauthenticated and returns `voter_name` for every vote (538), handing over the participant roster.
Note a nuance the claim omits: a signed-in attacker cannot spoof — `req.user.id` wins over req.body.email — so the attack requires the attacker to send the request unauthenticated (or with no session), which is trivially done. Alice, who voted while signed in, is keyed by her user id and is NOT overwritable by an email-keyed row; Alice, who voted by email (the common public-poll case), is.
fix: Do not accept a bare email as a write identity. Best: mint a per-invitee poll token (the BookingToken hashed-token pattern already exists at backend/services/scheduling/schedulingShared.js) and derive voter_key from the token. Minimum viable: make the email path insert-only — on a (option_id, voter_key) conflict from an unauthenticated caller, return 409 instead of updating (schedulingPublic.js:566-568), so an existing vote can never be silently rewritten, and stop returning voter_name from the public GET at 538.

evidence:
The unconditional carve-out the claim describes no longer exists. backend/services/scheduling/bookingService.js:167-174 now reads `if (mode === 'group') { hostUserId = ...; enforceExclusive = Math.max(1, eventType.seat_cap || 1) <= 1; }` with a comment naming exactly this hole ('A group event left at the default seat_cap=1 would otherwise fall through BOTH guards'). The arithmetic is correct in every case: seat_cap null/0/1 -> Math.max(1,1)=1 <= 1 -> enforce_exclusive TRUE, so the row is covered by Booking_no_overlap, whose predicate requires `enforce_exclusive = true` (backend/database/migrations/160_calendarly_bookings.sql:250-266); seat_cap >= 2 -> false, and the booking_enforce_group_cap trigger takes over, since its short-circuit only fires for `COALESCE(v_cap,1) <= 1` (163_calendarly_group_cap.sql:28). No configuration now falls between the two guards.
Residual (not the claimed defect, worth noting): enforce_exclusive is materialized on the row at INSERT (bookingService.js:214), so if a host later lowers seat_cap from 5 to 1, pre-existing rows keep enforce_exclusive=false and stay outside the exclusion constraint.
